--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page is the preface to Petrus Yvon’s treatise, following the title page. Yvon begins by outlining the core grievance of the Labadist movement: the perceived "decay" of contemporary Christianity compared to the purity of the early apostolic church. This section sets a prophetic and reformist tone, suggesting that the "fall of Antichristendom" is imminent because corruption has reached its peak.</meta>

# PREFACE.

\* 2

The great decay <note>original: "verval"</note> that one sees nowadays in Christendom must make us think seriously about its restoration. God will not always let things go in the manner in which they go almost everywhere today, or according to the flourish <note>In this context, "fleur" refers to the outward success or worldly fashion of the established churches.</note> that the spirit of this world has caused them to take, and still maintains. But He will eventually bring back once more the face or the form of the first Christianity; and the further one is now removed from it, so much closer may the time of renewal be. The **antichristendom** <note>For the Labadists, "Antichristendom" did not just refer to a single figure, but to the entire corrupt institutional church and worldly society that they believed had replaced true spiritual worship.</note> shall not always remain standing; and when shall it be nearest to its fall? Shall it not be then, when it shall fear it the least, and when it shall have climbed and been exalted as if to its fullness and highest step? And how clearly does one see that this is now fulfilled?

How much is the pure service of God, which consists in *spirit and in truth*, not degenerated, and how much is it not denied? In the **Papacy** <note>original: "Pausdom." A common 17th-century Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church.</note> such happens through manifold superstitious and idolatrous services that have been introduced there. And it happens also, whether within or without the Papacy, because everywhere one finds so few true worshippers who offer to God that service of the heart and spirit which He demands, and in which He alone has His divine pleasure.

Where does one see that living truth reigning that inspired the first Christians, and that made them Children of the highest Truth? How much is the same darkened by the errors of some, and by the irregularities of othe— <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page; it likely continues as "others" (d’anderen) on the following page.</note>

<summary>In this preface, Petrus Yvon laments the corruption of contemporary Christianity and calls for a restoration of the "first Christianity." He argues that the peak of institutional corruption signals that a divine renewal and the fall of "Antichristendom" are near.</summary>
<keywords>Christian restoration, Labadism, Antichristendom, Papacy, apostolic church, spiritual worship, religious decay, 17th-century theology</keywords>

# PREFACE.

...trampled underfoot, and even by those who, while most loudly professing them, clearly show by their deeds that they never truly held them in their hearts?

Where now is the life of those who were of *but one heart and one soul*? <note>A reference to Acts 4:32, describing the communal life and unity of the earliest Christians in Jerusalem, which the Labadists sought to emulate.</note> Where does one see that first purity of morals or of life in most of those who call themselves the Church of *Jesus Christ*? Where is the detachment <note>original: "losgemaektheyt." This refers to the spiritual and physical separation from worldly wealth and social status.</note> of those holy souls who, out of love for God, looked with joy upon the loss of their possessions, or who had more delight in distributing them to their brothers than the others had in receiving from their holy charity? Where is that complete consecration of oneself to *Jesus Christ* and His Kingdom, which shone so brightly at the beginning of Christianity? Where does that first zeal show itself, which burned in the hearts of those ancient believers? Is it not very rare and scarce? And is it not obvious that true love has grown cold everywhere, and that unrighteousness is overflowing, such that there is hardly true and living faith on earth, and that we have thus come again to the times of *Lot* and *Noah*, and finally to the last days, in which the world shall be judged and **Antichristendom** shall be cast down from its throne?

How little is the scepter of *Christ* feared by those who call themselves by His name? Where are the keys <note>A reference to the "Keys of the Kingdom," symbolizing the authority of the church to exercise discipline and exclude unrepentant sinners, a practice the Labadists felt the established churches had abandoned.</note> that He gave to His Church? And where does one see them being used properly? This pastoral guidance <note>original: "Herderlicke leydinge"</note> which for the—

->*<-

...[lives] so full of love, full of sweetness and faithfulness, and founded on the truth that is in **Jesus**, and which purely served the good of souls, the sanctification of the Church of God, and the glory of His Kingdom—does one find these in many places? Does one not even have great difficulty in finding even some traces of them? Where has that diligent and holy care gone, which one ought to have, to keep the world outside the Church, and to prevent the light and the darkness, righteousness and unrighteousness, **Christ** and **Belial** <note>A biblical name for the devil or the personification of worthlessness. The author is quoting 2 Corinthians 6:14-15, emphasizing the need for the "pure" Church to remain separate from the "corrupt" world.</note> from being mingled together, just as the words of God and His faithful servants so often and openly testify that such should not happen? And if things continue more and more in this way, what else could one expect but ultimate ruin and total destruction? Indeed, if God had not preserved and left some remnant <note>In the theology of the Labadists, the "remnant" refers to a small, chosen group of true believers who withdraw from a corrupt society to start a new, holy community.</note>, which, finally being gathered by His Hand out of the scattering, shall be as the seed of a new people and serve for the renewal of the earth, one would have nothing else to expect than that God would do to so-called **Christendom** what He once did to **Sodom** and **Gomorra**, namely, that He would utterly destroy and overthrow it.

The sad and lamentable state in which the **Reformed** <term>Gereformeerde: followers of the Calvinist tradition</term> in **France**, in **Poland**, in **Hungary**, and almost everywhere have been brought by the righteous judgment or the chastisement of God, ought...

<summary>The author laments the corruption of contemporary Christianity, arguing that the lack of distinction between the holy and the worldly will lead to divine destruction unless a "remnant" of true believers is gathered. He cites the contemporary persecution of Protestants across Europe as evidence of God's judgment.</summary>

# PREFACE.

->*<-

...should it <note>Referring to the "ultimate ruin" mentioned on the previous page.</note> not cause **Lutheranism** to tremble, given that the same is no less corrupt in regards to the lives of its followers, or the way in which things are conducted therein, and is certainly more surrounded by gloom and darkness in respect to its Doctrine? And what does the **Papacy** <term>Pauſdom: The Roman Catholic Church</term> not have to expect, which is as the source from which all the corruptions of the others have sprung, and which, by providing the example to the others, possesses these corruptions in their full measure?

God speaks through those heavy blows of His Hand, which are presently stretched out, especially over the **Reformed** in **France**, of whom the ruin and the voluntary apostasy of most is terrifying.

This is a touchstone <note>A "touchstone" (Dutch: *toetsteen*) was a hard stone used to test the purity of precious metals; here it refers to a spiritual test of genuine faith.</note> for all **Reformed**. For since those in **France** are no worse than the others, we may well believe that people everywhere would do the same as they, if one found oneself in the same circumstances; and that

# PREFACE.

->* 4<-

> "consequently, courage and faith are the
> rarest things in the entire world.
> Finally, it is a matter that speaks and says, that
> God is causing the heart of this people to melt, and
> wishes to let the same sink into the earth, in
> order soon to prepare another, new people for Himself."

It is then certain that God calls and obliges His own, however deeply they may have fallen asleep, in all states and in all places, to wake up. And He calls them, beyond all doubt, to first apply themselves with all their heart to their own **sanctification** <term>heyligmakinge: the process of being made holy or consecrated to God's service</term> and **renewal**; and then afterward to respond with faithfulness and zeal to that which the Lord might demand of them for the help of others, giving them an example of that to which God wants them to devote themselves with a perfect heart and soul.

There are some whom God has pulled out from the mass of the world and the sinners, and others who still remain therein—indeed, believe they must remain there. The former can suitably provide an example to the others of that to which they should at least strive to restore things, according to their state and in the place where they find themselves. For why would one remain there otherwise, if one cannot do one's duty there, if one cannot keep oneself unspotted there, and if one is as if forced there—against the express command of the **Mouth of the Lord** <note>original: *Mont des Heeren*; a biblical idiom referring to God's direct word or commandment</note>—to become a partaker in the sins of others?

Since God, through His **goodness** <note>original: *goetheyt*</note>, has now placed us among the number of those whom He more fully—

<meta>This page continues the preface by Petrus Yvon. It completes the sentence from the previous page regarding the believers' deliverance from the world and outlines the specific mission of the Labadist community: personal adherence to the Gospel and the spiritual restoration of others.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...[from] the bonds of this world, we feel ourselves particularly obliged to these two things; first, to faithfully regulate ourselves according to the pure truth of the **Gospel** <term>Evangeliums: the message of Christ's salvation and the teachings of the New Testament</term>, and according to the example that Jesus has given to His People on **Mount Zion** <note>original: *Berg Sion*; a biblical reference to the spiritual city of God or the true, gathered church of believers</note>. And secondly, to help others as much as we can, so that they may see and feel their downfall, and may rise out of the same through the powerful grace of the Lord. This is the **aim** <note>original: *wit*; literally "the white," referring to the center of a target</note> of our **Christian community** <term>Christelicke gemeynschap: the Labadist fellowship, which sought to recreate the communal life of the early apostles</term>; it is there that our guidance, through the grace of the Lord, tends: and it is for that reason that we, not being able to speak to everyone, make known through writing that which we believe to be necessary and useful for the good of the souls whom God wants us to serve, and which could greatly serve for the **Reforming** <term>Reformeeringe: the process of restoration or spiritual renewal</term> of that which, according to the general consent of all, is so greatly deformed and fallen almost everywhere.

It is according to these insights that this Book now comes to light, in hope that the Lord in His time will pour out His blessing upon it to the glory of His Name. We present therein the truths that have touched and convinced us, and according to which we have felt obliged to earnestly reform ourselves, and which certainly can also be useful for those who shall be zealous for the **House of God** <term>Huys Gods: a reference to the church as a spiritual household or temple of believers</term>, even if they might not agree with all our views, and for the present might hold and walk a different path than ours.

<summary>Yvon explains the dual purpose of their community: living strictly by the Gospel and helping others recognize their spiritual decay. He presents this book as a tool for the "Reformation" of a church that is widely acknowledged as fallen and deformed.</summary>

<keywords>Gospel, Mount Zion, Labadist community, spiritual reformation, House of God, Petrus Yvon, sanctification, church decay</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface by Petrus Yvon, moving from the general mission of the Labadist community to the specific necessity of church discipline and the sanctity of the Lord's Supper. # PREFACE.

<sig>* 5</sig>

**Church discipline** <term>Kerkelicke discipline: the practice of maintaining moral and spiritual order within a congregation, including the correction or exclusion of members who live in open sin</term> is almost no longer known, although the first martyrs at the time of the **Reformation** <term>Reformatie: the 16th-century movement to reform the Catholic Church, which led to the establishment of Protestantism</term>, and among others that great martyr **Anne du Bourg** <note>Anne du Bourg (1521–1559) was a French magistrate executed for his Protestant beliefs; his courage was a major inspiration for early Reformed believers</note>, assured that it is one of the glorious marks of the Church. Holy things are almost no longer reserved for the Holy; on the contrary, one sees that such people are often kept away from them, while at the same time these things are openly thrown before the unholy. **Christian Fellowship** <term>Christelicke Gemeynschap: the spiritual and communal bond shared by true believers</term> is expressed to all without distinction, and is thereby prostituted; and the **Holy Supper** <term>Avontmael: the Eucharist or Communion, viewed by the Labadists as a meal only for the truly converted</term>, which is its most expressive and final seal, is mostly given to those who have no fellowship at all with Jesus Christ and true Christians. These are matters that go to our heart, and about which one will see our sentiments declared according to truth in this Book.

One should not find it strange that we give this title, *The Holy for the Holy*, to this work, and thereby indicate that the Holy Supper is instituted for them alone. All true Christians are sanctified in Christ, and made into **Saints** <note>original: *Heyligen*; here used in the biblical sense of "set apart" or "consecrated" believers rather than canonized figures</note> through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, of whom they are Temples and living instruments. This is indeed like a **paradox** <note>original: *wonderspreuke*; literally a "wonder-saying" or a statement that seems contradictory to common sense</note> in the ears of fleshly men; but they cannot prevent themselves, however, from seeing with their own eyes that the Apostles constantly gave the name of "Saints" to all the first Christians.

> ,, *I am holy*, says **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential early Christian theologian</note>, spoken
> ,, by a true Believer, is no vain and
> ,, haughty word of a proud man; but it is a

<summary>Yvon laments the loss of church discipline and the opening of the Lord's Supper to the unworthy, arguing that the "Holy Supper" is intended strictly for those sanctified by the Holy Spirit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface by Petrus Yvon, following a discussion on the liturgical formula "The Holy is for the Holy" and the necessity of believers acknowledging their sanctification through Christ. # PREFACE.

...which, having already been touched upon or treated by us elsewhere, had to be inserted here again as necessary and in their proper place. In the fourth part of this book, where one will see the **Doctrine of the Christian Church** in the first centuries, one will occasionally be able to find certain expressions or words that are currently out of use among Protestants. But it will be enough to note regarding this that these should not be taken according to the abuse that was later made of them, but according to their first use, and according to the intention of those ancient Teachers of the Church who first employed them. And although we have presented the testimonies of the **Church Fathers** <note>Original: "Out-vaderen"; the influential theologians and writers of the early Christian Church whose works established early orthodoxy.</note> at length, we do not, however, adopt everything—down to the smallest details—as our own. It is sufficient that one grants the principal points, the substance, and the general objective thereof, so as to be compelled to confess that we have deviated very far from the ancient strictness of the Saints regarding sinners; and that our view and our practice are abundantly confirmed by Christian Antiquity. Furthermore, **Reverend [D.] Koelman** <note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695) was a prominent Dutch Reformed minister and writer. Initially a friend of the Labadist movement, he later became a critic, leading to the theological exchanges mentioned here.</note> will be able to see through this book that we did not promise in vain in our **Treatise on Baptism** that we would treat the **Holy Supper** <term>H. Avontmael: also known as Holy Communion or the Eucharist; the author focuses here on the requirements for participation.</term> thoroughly and extensively in another place. And even if he might not notice it, certainly others, reading the same, will see without effort that what might still actually need to be further clarified and settled between him and us is sufficiently defined and dealt with here.

<summary>In this concluding section of the preface, the author defends the use of early Church terminology and asserts that his views on church discipline and the Holy Supper are supported by ancient Christian tradition and resolve ongoing disputes with Reverend Koelman.</summary>

The title "The Holy for the Saints" reflects a common 17th-century view that the sacrament was reserved exclusively for those deemed spiritually prepared or "holy."</meta>

Since we specifically intend in this book to deal only with the correct distribution and reception of this great **Seal of the New Covenant** <term>Seal of the New Covenant: A theological term for a Sacrament, viewed as a physical "seal" that confirms and guarantees the spiritual promises made by God to humanity.</term>, we shall not enter into a detailed investigation of the various opinions that today leave the so-called Christian people so divided on this matter. A large portion—which is again divided into two groups—believes they hold fast to the essence of this mystery <note>original: "verborgenthept"</note> well and properly by believing that what they generally eat and drink (even without faith, a holy life, or love) is Christ himself and his substantial Body, even though their works testify that Christ is infinitely far from their hearts and souls. 

Another group imagines that true Believers, when they celebrate the **Lord's Supper** <note>original: "Avontmael," literally "Evening Meal."</note>, are only called and obligated to be mindful of what Jesus did and suffered for them. Often, these people do not have the slightest living impression of the true and real communion <note>original: "gemeynschap"</note> that the hearts and souls of the true Members of Jesus Christ have with Him, nor of the share they receive in His Death and Life through their grafting into Him, through their "putting on" of Him in all His divine mysteries, through their conformity with Him, and through that which they express in their lives from the impression they have received of Jesus in their hearts. Certainly, when they remember that Christ gave the Supper only to His Disciples, they must also refuse the same to those who do not in any way display the identifying signs or hallmarks of such discipleship.

**Jesus** instituted the Lord's Supper <term>Avontmael: literally "Evening Meal," the standard Dutch term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term> after He had fully exposed Judas, had ceased speaking of him, and had said to him clearly and openly, "You have said so," thereby answering his question, "Is it I, Rabbi, who shall betray you?" How is it also to be understood or believed that Christ, in giving the bread and the wine to Judas as signs and seals of His Body, His Blood, and all His benefits, could have said, "This is my body which is broken for you, and my blood which is shed for you"? These following words, "Truly I say to you, that I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine, until that day when I shall drink it new with you in the Kingdom of God," could just as little be applied to him. Did Jesus drink those things with Judas, or shall He drink them with him? Did He also die for him? Or did He shed His Blood for the forgiveness of his sins? One clearly sees that this cannot be said, as Hilary of Poitiers <note>A 4th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church; the reference is to his "In Evangelium Matthaei Commentarius"</note> in Canon 30 on Matthew has very well noted.

### CHAPTER 10.

**That the Lord Jesus, by forbidding the giving of the holy to dogs and the throwing of pearls before swine, shows His will that the unholy and those who partake of the Lord’s Supper without proper discernment shall be excluded from the same.**

<margin>Matthew 7:6.</margin>
When the Lord Jesus gave His Disciples the rules by which they were to guide themselves, and declared His holy will to them, He spoke these remarkable words: Do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you in pieces.

By "the holy" and "the pearls" of which the Lord speaks, one may and must certainly understand the most holy and exalted truths of the Gospel and of grace, as well as those truths which most powerfully provoke or oppose our corrupt nature. These truths should not be easily presented to those who can do nothing but misuse them, but should instead be applied to suitable listeners with proper discernment. ### CHAPTER XI.

#### Confirmation of the same truth through the words of Christ <note>original: "Christi"</note> which are read in Matthew 15, verse 26.

Our supreme Lord and Master says in the 15th chapter of Matthew some words that are no less worthy of attention than those we considered in the previous chapter. <margin>It is v. 26.</margin> The same read thus: *It is not fitting to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs.* <note>The Dutch "hondekens" is a diminutive, reflecting the Greek *kunariois* (little dogs or puppies) used in this Gospel passage.</note> Regarding this we must note: 1. That Jesus said this in view of a miracle that the Canaanite woman <note>A woman from the region of Phoenicia who was not Jewish, often cited as a model of persistent faith.</note> requested of Him. 2. That He initially showed Himself reluctant to grant the same to a soul who came to Him in sincerity and with trust; a proof of this is that He gave her the desired good after He had let her pray for it once more, and had tested not only her faith, but her humility (which made her confess that she was worthy of the name "little dog") and her steadfast love, which she showed in the persistence of her request, and of which He received an excellent proof.

From this surely flow three things that serve our subject. ### CHAPTER XII.

**That the entire 5th Chapter of the 1st Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians proves that the Holy Supper is not for the wicked; and that they, accordingly, may not come to it, nor be rightfully admitted.**

Although we will not now cite the various words that could be gathered from the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles on this matter, we cannot omit presenting those of the Apostle **Paul** from 1 Corinthians 5. All those who uphold the necessity of the **Discipline of the Church** <term>Church Discipline: The practice of correcting or excluding members of a church who persist in open sin, intended to lead the sinner to repentance and protect the community's purity.</term> have especially and with great foundation proven the same through these Apostolic arguments against their opponents.

From the beginning of the Chapter, Paul sharply rebukes the **Congregation** <note>The early Christian community in the city of Corinth.</note> of Corinth because they had not cut off that wicked man quickly enough and removed him from their midst. In this, the Pastors and **Overseers** <term>Elders or leaders: Those responsible for the spiritual oversight and governance of the local church.</term> whose duty this had been, had made themselves very guilty before God and the eyes of His Spirit.

Therefore, he declares God's will on this matter; he expressly and absolutely commands the Corinthians on the Lord's behalf to purge out the old leaven and remove it from the Congregation, whose general Body had become a new dough through the Lord's grace.

### Chapter XV.

That those who wander and those who are ignorant of the essential points of Christianity, and in particular do not know Jesus Christ nor believe in Him, must not approach or be admitted to the Holy Supper; and what the true knowledge of Christ, and faith in Him, entails.

It is certain and is admitted by nearly everyone that the Holy Supper <term>Holy Supper: The Dutch *Avontmael* refers to the sacrament of Communion or the Eucharist, which the author argues must be protected from those who lack understanding.</term> must not be given to those who neither believe nor confess the sound Doctrine <note>original: *geſonde Leere*</note>, since this may only happen to those who are at least of one and the same confession and religion; and this is denied by no one except those who wander very far from the truth. It is also no less certain that those who come to the Supper must be so far instructed in the Doctrine of truth that they have, at the very least, sufficient knowledge of the essential points and foundations of the same. Even the most lax <note>The original Dutch *pverlooſte* (over-loose) suggests teachers who are overly permissive or lacking in strictness.</note> Teachers do not deny this, as they acknowledge that the ignorant are among the first who must be kept away from the Supper.

And quite rightly so; for if one does not understand one's Confession <term>Confession: The *Belijdenis*, a formal statement of religious belief or a creed that a member of the church is expected to uphold.</term>, how can one then believe it or rightly profess it? Or would it be enough to say that one believes what the Church believes? Would those who bear the name of "Reformed" <note>This refers to the *Gereformeerde* Church, the official state-sanctioned Calvinist church in the Dutch Republic.</note> be satisfied with such a faith, which is called a blind, implicit <note>The Dutch *ingewichelt* literally means "enfolded" or "wrapped up." It refers to "implicit faith," a concept often criticized by Protestants where a person simply accepts church dogma without understanding it personally.</note>, and "everyone's" faith?

->*Second and Third Point of the saving knowledge of Jesus Christ.*<-

Regarding the second part—namely, what He has done and suffered for His own; and the third—what He does or works through His Spirit and grace in them and with them; these are no less important and essential. The knowledge of these things is so much more necessary today as Satan, with all his cunning, seeks to destroy them or make them fruitless. He does this especially by separating one from the other, making some content themselves only with the second and reject the third, while others apparently embrace the third exclusively <term>exclusively: The original Dutch "puer" suggests embracing one aspect purely or strictly while neglecting the other.</term> but do not accept—even oppose—the second. Thus, he deceives everyone through that vain and false pretense, as if what they profess were enough to be saved. But true Christians, and those who stand in the teaching of Christ, are far from wishing to divide Him. They embrace Him entirely, just as He was given to them by the Father. Their faith extends to all His mysteries <term>mysteries: The Dutch "Verborgentheden" refers to spiritual truths or divine secrets that are hidden from the ungodly but revealed to believers.</term> and works. They know that He died only for those whom He causes to die to the world and to themselves; and that one also thinks in vain that they can die to themselves unless they have a living faith in His death, and through that same faith place their trust in the mystery of His cross, or in Him as crucified and died.

<margin>PART I.</margin> say? Since at present no one may come to it except only the mature persons who can give proof of their faith and of the state of their souls before God, it is evident that the **<term>Teachers</term>** <note>original: "Leeraers," refers here to the ministers or clergy who oversaw the spiritual life of the congregation</note> who do not examine them in this regard are entirely without excuse; indeed, they make themselves guilty of the sin that such people commit if they take this holy Sacrament unworthily. The **<term>Lord’s Supper</term>** <note>original: "Avontmael"</note> signifies and seals in substance the same as—indeed, even more than—**<term>Baptism</term>** <note>original: "Doop"</note>. For just as Baptism may not be administered except only to those who are regarded as being made alive in Christ, so the holy Lord’s Supper must also not be given except only to those who demonstrate that they have made some progress in that life of grace, communicated to the soul in its **<term>rebirth</term>** <note>original: "wedergeboorte"</note>. The first of these Sacraments relates to the birth of the new creature, and the other to its nourishment and growth through the eating of a more solid food; as the Teachers of the first centuries <note>A reference to the Church Fathers of the early Christian era</note> have often said and shown. One is instituted and used to seal someone's first entry into the Church; and the other must only be administered to those who have already spent some time in the same, and have lived worthily of the One who led them into it. One must therefore certainly attempt to distinguish who those are that may be nourished with the Lord’s Supper, which the Saints of old called the *food of the strong*, just as they compared the administration of Baptism to the milk with which little children are fed.

...is a great abomination, just like one who condemns the righteous <note>This continues a quote from Proverbs 17:15: "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the Lord."</note>. If this is said regarding **civil law**, which only looks upon man and human affairs, how much more must it be said regarding **Ecclesiastical law** <term>Ecclesiastical law: The internal legal systems and principles used to govern a church's organization and discipline.</term>, which directly concerns itself with God and holy things? Just as the soul is greater than the body, so also, without doubt, must everything concerning the soul be weightier and more carefully considered. God sees everything; one must not imagine that while He finds secular Judges—who through human motives hold and declare the guilty to be innocent—to be an abomination, He does not find even more of an abomination in Church Judges who commit the same sin, by the same principle and for the same end. With God—who in the quoted words so greatly condemns partiality <note>original: *aennemen der personen*. Literally "the accepting of persons," a biblical term for showing favoritism or bias in judgment.</note>—there is no partiality at all. PART I. THE HOLY

### CHAPTER XIX.

->Convincing and tangible proofs that one must not celebrate the <term>Lord’s Supper: Also called Communion or the Eucharist, a sacrament where bread and wine are shared to remember Christ's death.</term> with the unworthy, nor with a congregation in which the same are not barred from the Lord’s Table.<-

Before we finish the first part of this book, we shall here set forth and establish our views in more detail regarding those <term>Believers: In this context, those who are considered truly converted or "godly," as opposed to "nominal" Christians who are only members in name.</term> who find no liberty of conscience to <term>communicate: To participate in the sacrament of Communion (the Lord's Supper).</term> with such congregations, the majority of which clearly consists of worldly and often scandalous people. These are congregations where one knows and is convinced that, in the admission of <term>Members: Formal members of a church congregation who have been granted the right to participate in the sacraments.</term>, they do not believe themselves obliged to ensure that the persons give sufficient reason to be regarded as Believers, <term>Born-again: Refers to the spiritual rebirth or "regeneration" that the author considers essential for a true Christian.</term>, and true Christians. Instead, they accept the unworthy, and even such people of whom it is generally admitted that they ought not to be accepted. Regarding this, we believe that Believers not only truly have the freedom to abstain from holding the Lord’s Supper with such people or congregations, but that this is their true duty—especially when they see that the other means applied by themselves or others for the improvement of this prevailing and deep-rooted evil are and remain entirely useless and fruitless.

From that which predominates in the mixture, the names are derived. <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῶ πλεονεκτῶντος ἐν τῇ κράσει γíνονται αἱ προσηγορíαι."</note> Galen.</margin> b Babel, or Jerusalem, according to that head <note>The defining characteristic or governing spirit.</note>. ### CHAPTER I.

General answer to the difficulty raised concerning the knowing and distinguishing of the state of those who shall be admitted to Church communion and the holy Lord's Supper.

The greatest and most general difficulty <note>In this context, "difficulty" refers to a formal theological objection or a "stumbling block" in reasoning.</note> brought against the preceding truths is that one cannot know who the true Believers are, and who, consequently, are truly worthy to be admitted to Church communion and to the Lord’s Supper <term>Avontmael: the Dutch term for the Sacrament of Holy Communion, literally meaning "Evening Meal"</term> which is the seal thereof. It is sometimes added that one is not obligated to arrive at this knowledge and distinction, and further that one should not even undertake such a task, under the pretext that there are or can be hypocrites and pretenders in the Church, and that one can err in the distinguishing of persons, since there can be true Believers without them appearing as such outwardly. It is certain that there is no real, substantial difficulty at the core of what is brought against us in this matter. Nevertheless, most people present it as being very well-founded, and not only as something worthy of being considered, but even as sufficient reason to suspend and restrain the holy stirrings of zeal <note>The word "yver" (zeal) here refers to a passionate commitment to religious purity and the honor of God.</note> that can sometimes arise in the heart. The learned and the unlearned, the great and the small, the profane and the lukewarm, the pious and the impious, the faint-hearted and the indifferent, those who are prejudiced and those who cling to their own opinions, interests, and honor, and finally, the vehement and the embittered—all believe they have no firmer wall nor stronger shield with which to defend themselves against the truth, and to prevent themselves from being compelled and overcome by it. It is therefore quite right that we strip this defense away from them and show clearly that those who allow themselves to be held back from fulfilling their duty are without excuse <note>original: "onveronschuldelick"</note> before God and before those who possess as much rightful zeal for His honor as they do sincere and true love for His Church and Christ's Kingdom.

In general, we need only to observe that if it were impossible to know whether someone is in a state to receive the Lord's Supper <term>Avontmael: the Sacrament of the Eucharist</term> properly, or whether they are unworthy to approach it according to the laws of God, then not only would all the words spoken by God on this matter be useless, but it would also be in vain to have Consistories <term>Consistorien: the governing council of a local Reformed church</term>, Elders <term>Ouderlingen: church officers charged with the spiritual oversight of the congregation</term>, and Shepherds or Leaders to

<margin>PART II.</margin>...to have <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: "...it would be in vain to have ministers..."</note>, in order to regulate everything in the congregation <term>Gemeynte: the local assembly or community of believers</term>, to take care of holy things, to watch that they are not prostituted and profaned, and to provide everything the congregation needs to keep it in good condition and preserve it from corruption. Otherwise, one should no longer speak of **church discipline** <term>kerckelicke tucht: the formal process of correcting or excluding members to maintain the purity of the church</term> or of the government of the Church, and one would have to strip the ministers <note>original: "Predikanten"</note> of all the **authority** they possess—authority they certainly would not want to lose.

Although many of them usually argue that they do not know their people and *cannot* know them when they are urged to deal with each individual according to **conscience** and as each person’s spiritual state requires; nevertheless, they do not fail to show in practice that they believe they know very well who is worthy of being **censured** or **suspended** from the Lord’s Supper <term>Avontmael: the Sacrament of the Eucharist</term> whenever they see fit to exercise their authority. This they do even against the godly, who often, instead of being censured or suspended, should rather be supported and praised. In those instances, they assert their office, their duty, and the **authority** that the **servants of Christ** have received from Him, as well as the care they are permitted to exercise so that everything proceeds orderly in His house, and so that those who have sinned, spoken wrongly, or misbehaved may be restrained, suspended, and barred from the enjoyment of the holy signs <note>The "holy signs" refer to the bread and wine used in Communion.</note>. They therefore admit, in such cases, that they *can* recognize those who deserve to be excluded; indeed, in such circumstances, they maintain that the ordinances <note>original: "ordonnantien"</note> and words of God concerning this matter are clear and—

1. That the faith they possess is not a fruit of **election** <term>election <note>The Calvinist doctrine that God chooses specific individuals for salvation before the world began.</note></term>, nor of the **saving grace** of Jesus Christ, because they are not among the chosen and do not attain salvation.

Finally, it is true that **temporary faith** <term>temporary faith <note>original Dutch: "tijtgeloof"; a belief that is sincere in the moment but lacks a root in grace and fails during trials.</note></term> does not realistically and in truth change the person, as they never fundamentally become a **new creature** <term>new creature <note>A person spiritually reborn through divine grace.</note></term>.

<margin>2 Peter 2:22</margin>
The washed sow remains a sow; she retains her sow-like nature, and through that nature—which she never lost—she returns again to wallowing in the mire from which she was pulled. Yet, although this is so, it is nonetheless certain that without an **extraordinary and very special light** <note>A supernatural discernment or revelation from God.</note>, such a condition cannot be perceived in them; and even most of those enlightened from Heaven have for a time believed, and had great reason to believe, that these people were fundamentally what they were later found not to be. ### Chapter VI.

The nature of the certainty of the knowledge that one can have concerning **Communicants** <term>Communicants: 'Communicanten', those who participate in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper.</term> or **Table-companions** <term>Table-companions: 'Disgenoten', a synonym for those sharing the fellowship of the communion table.</term>. That it is not infallible, nor is it necessary that it should be.

We stated at the beginning that in order to fully clarify this matter, it must be observed what kind of certainty **Shepherds** <term>Shepherds: 'Herders', a traditional term for pastors or ministers leading a congregation.</term> have or can have regarding their **Flocks**; this is what we must now address.

It is clear, first, that this knowledge is not infallible, nor is its certainty beyond all misconception. God alone is the infallible Being, and there is no knowledge but His alone that is perfect and unshakable—being always the same and as infinite as His Essence is. The knowledge of **Angels** and the **Blessed** <note>The 'Blessed' (Gelucksalige) refers to the souls of the faithful departed who are now in heaven.</note>, although it is true, very clear, and far-reaching, is nonetheless confined within certain limits; and if they wished to go beyond those limits, or extend them further than what God reveals or proposes to them, they would surely err. This is even more evident and certain regarding the knowledge that humans possess here on Earth, however holy and enlightened they are or may be. Experience has also taught that they can err—indeed, at times they have erred—not only regarding themselves and their own actions, but also regarding others, and in their public dealings concerning the Church or the **People of God**. 

<margin>Numbers 20: 11, 12.</margin> 
Thus Moses erred in the striking <note>original: 'slaen'. This refers to the biblical account where Moses struck the rock twice in anger instead of speaking to it as God commanded.</note>

<summary>This page introduces Chapter VI, arguing that the spiritual judgment of church leaders is inherently fallible. Only God possesses absolute knowledge, while even angels, saints, and biblical figures like Moses are subject to limitations and error.</summary>

**There are two kinds of certainty: one is absolute, and the other is not. And this [latter] is that which one calls moral certainty** <term>moral certainty: a level of certainty that is sufficient for making decisions in human affairs, based on high probability and reliable evidence rather than mathematical proof</term>**, and which we apply to spiritual things, as it is often just as great—indeed, even firmer—than any other moral certainty is. This certainty is not exactly the same as that which one has, for example, through the physical senses, such as sight and hearing. But it is evident on the one hand that the senses help to strengthen this certainty, because one hears the good or evil words by which—** <margin>Matthew 12:37.</margin> **Jesus says one is lawfully judged; and one sees the good works of the good, and the evil works of the evil; so that through the sight of these things, one can judge the faith of the one, or the unbelief and deceit of the other.** On the other hand, it is certain that the **inner and new man** <note>original: 'inwendigen en nieuwen mensch'; a reference to the spiritually regenerated person described by the Apostle Paul.</note> has his **spiritual senses** <term>spiritual senses: the internal capacity of a believer to perceive divine or spiritual realities, analogous to how the body uses physical senses</term>, by which he perceives spiritual objects. He has his vision and spiritual perception, by which he ordinarily penetrates deeper than the physical eye can see. He has his spiritual hearing for the same purpose. He has a supernatural taste, which makes him taste and savor that which is sprinkled and salted with the **salt of wisdom** <note>original: 'sout der wijsheyt'; a biblical metaphor for grace, purity, and spiritual insight in speech and conduct.</note> and with the spirit, and gives him a loathing for the other; and he often has a spiritual feeling, which allows him to see more intimately into objects those things which do not appear at first, but which he later becomes aware of. <margin>PART II.</margin> I have denied that and maintain, along with <term>Mr. Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar. His "Demonstratio Evangelica" attempted to prove the truths of Christianity using a rigorous method similar to geometric proofs.</note></term> in his <term>Evangelical Demonstration <note>original: "Evangelische Demonstratie," referring to the Latin work *Demonstratio Evangelica* (1679).</note></term>, that it <note>referring to moral certainty</note> sometimes goes further and is more well-founded than **Mathematical** or **Mathematical** <note>The original uses two synonyms: the Dutch "Wiskonstige" and the Latinate "Matematische."</note> certainty, which is nevertheless held to be the clearest and most indubitable of all.

Absolute certainty looks upon things that are of such a nature that they cannot be otherwise, and the knowledge of which is consequently infallible. But a thing is said to be "likely" or <term>probable <note>original: "waerschijnelick of probabel."</note></term> when one has some reason to think that it is so, or can be such as one judges it to be; or when one finds just as much reason to think it as not to think it. This remains true even if there might be just as much—indeed, sometimes more—reason which, if weighed, would cause one to suspend judgment and give cause to believe that what one considers probable in a subject is not actually there. This is what probability entails, and it goes only so far. 

But <term>moral certainty <note>original: "moreele sekerheyt." In the 17th century, this was a technical term for a degree of proof that is sufficient for all practical purposes and leaves no room for reasonable doubt, even if it is not "mathematically" impossible for it to be false.</note></term> undeniably goes much further, since it has as its object only those things about which one has incomparably more reason to believe than to doubt that they are in accordance with what one thinks of them. Indeed, the proofs for the certainty of these things are so clear and powerful that, after having examined everything, one cannot help but give one’s consent to them. This can be seen in the previously cited examples of things which we have shown are known with certainty, though not infallibly.

<summary>The author argues that moral certainty—the kind used to judge a person's faith—is a higher and more reliable form of knowledge than mere probability, even comparing its strength to mathematical certainty.</summary>

In this, it differs from the certainty of **Physics** and **Mathematical demonstrations**, which properly serve to examine the truths of their own order, both in themselves and in their mutual relations. And it is this moral certainty that we attribute to the knowledge that <term>Men of God <note>In this context, referring to the ministers and elders responsible for "fencing the table" or vetting the spiritual maturity of the congregation.</note></term> can have regarding the spiritual state of those persons who are declared and accepted as **Members of the Church**. These are individuals believed to be in a state to enjoy the **Lord’s Supper** for their salvation, and not to their own judgment and condemnation <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:29, warning that those who eat the bread or drink the cup unworthily "eat and drink judgment to themselves."</note>. This certainty is also sufficient to maintain ecclesiastical fellowship with someone, just as it is sufficient for civil fellowship and for the everyday communion that ordinary pious people hold with one another. For the knowledge they have of each other—upon which their mutual fellowship and love is grounded—likewise has only (as has been said and shown) a moral, and not an absolute or infallible, certainty.

Furthermore, if one follows the principles of <term>Domine Koelman <note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695), a Dutch minister and a leader of the "Nadere Reformatie" (Dutch Second Reformation), known for his strict views on church purity and liturgy.</note></term> and <term>Brakel <note>Wilhelmus à Brakel (1635–1711), an influential Dutch theologian whose work "The Christian's Reasonable Service" became a cornerstone of Dutch Reformed piety. And it is certainly in vain to argue against this / that they <note>The prophecies of a pure Church.</note> can be understood and explained if one applies them to the invisible Church <note>A theological concept referring to the "true" body of believers known only to God, as opposed to the "visible Church" seen in earthly institutions.</note> / or to the Elect <note>Those chosen by God for salvation.</note> and Believers who are mingled among the others / although the bulk / and without comparison the largest part / yes the general body of the assemblies among which they are scattered and ordinarily as if stifled <note>original: "verstickt"; often used to describe wheat being choked by weeds.</note> / is composed of worldly people / who have neither godliness / nor true knowledge and fear of the Lord. ->Third general proof, taken from the words of the Evangelists, and from the Teaching of Jesus Christ our Lord himself.<-

A third general proof of the same truth—namely, that under the Gospel one indeed cannot or must not recognize anyone as a member of the Church except with regard to the conversion of the heart and the renewal of life—is taken from the manner in which the new People were prepared for Jesus Christ, and from the foundation upon which He Himself grounded His Church. PART III. The life of these **Believers** and **Christians** was indeed a general triumph over desire <note>The original Dutch "begeerlickheyt" refers to worldly lusts, greed, or the craving for material things.</note> and a complete overthrow of the world and its sinful spirit. Besides this, it is certain that they not only dedicated everything from their hearts to **Jesus Christ** and his kingdom, but they were moreover in danger at every moment of losing their honor, their freedom, and even their lives, simply by confessing that they were **Disciples** of **Jesus Christ**, against whom the **Jewish** and **Heathen** <note>original: "Heydensche"; referring to the non-Jewish, Greco-Roman world.</note> world was so immediately opposed and hostile. Who can deny that these **Christians** were constantly occupied with sowing the knowledge and love of **Jesus Christ** in all places and extending his kingdom everywhere? Was this not the sole and holy drive of their hearts? Was everything else not as nothing to them in comparison? And did they spare any of their possessions to achieve the goal of their desire?

Furthermore, it should be noted that this divine drive and that pure and holy fire were not only found in some **Members** of this <margin>Acts 2: 41, 44-47. 4: 31-37. 6: 31.</margin> **Church**, but that this entire **Body** <note>Refers to the "Body of Christ," a theological term for the collective community of believers.</note> was, as it were, consumed by it. ### Chapter X.

->Examination and resolution of that which is brought forward from Baptism and the ministry of John the Baptist against the teaching confirmed in this Third Part, as well as in the First Part of this book.<-

We said at the beginning of this Third Part that we intended to show what the foundation was for admitting persons to the communion of the Christian People <note>The "Christian People" (Christen Volk) refers to the true body of believers or the Church.</note> and the enjoyment of the holy things which are established for them alone. We also stated that we would demonstrate that Holy Scripture constantly teaches that, in order to have a part and communion in this People, one must share in the Spirit of grace and rebirth. Consequently, the fruits of that Spirit alone make known who belongs to this People, or who is in a state to be counted among them, and the proofs and seals <note>In this context, "proofs and seals" likely refers to the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which were historically viewed as outward signs (seals) of inward grace.</note>

<margin>Chapter 10.</margin> [it cannot be] said that the Baptism of John was merely a bare ceremony, and without any fruit of the Spirit in those who received it properly; for by what would one prove that, and how much reason does one not have to say and establish the opposite? ->*That nonetheless it cannot be denied that there is a distinction between the two.*<-

However, it cannot well be denied that there is some distinction between these two kinds of Baptism. Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a prominent Lutheran theologian who wrote a famous critique of the Catholic Council of Trent</note> says in his *Examination of the Council of Trent* <note>original: "Examen over 't Concilie van Trenten"</note> these noteworthy words: <margin>Part 2, on Baptism, page 65.</margin> That there has been some distinction between the Baptism of John and that of Jesus Christ, such is agreed upon by all Ancient Teachers <note>The Church Fathers</note>, and the Scripture indicates it; only it must be seen wherein the same consists, and how far it actually goes. And before this he does not hesitate to say: I see that Augustine <note>original: "Augustinus"</note>, who believed that the Baptism of John was different from that of Christ, gives reasons for it that are not to be despised; for without speaking of Acts 19 <note>original: "Act. 19."; referring to the passage where disciples of John are baptized again in the name of Jesus</note>, upon which he particularly dwells, it is no small proof of their distinction that when Christ began to baptize through his Disciples—yes, even after the Believers throughout the whole world were baptized with his Baptism—nonetheless the Baptism of John always retained its own name, and was constantly called the Baptism of John, in distinction from the Baptism [of Christ].

<margin>Chapter X.</margin>
Disciples, having heard the teaching of the **Apostle** <note>the Apostle Paul</note>, were truly baptized by his order and direction. After Paul—says **Diodati** <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a renowned Protestant theologian and translator</note>—had extensively instructed them on the regard that **John** <note>John the Baptist</note> had for **Jesus Christ**, they formally received baptism in the Name of Christ; for it was not absurd to confirm the extraordinary Baptism of John through the ordinary and more explicit baptism of Christ; since God indeed willed that those who had received the seal of the Old Covenant, Circumcision, should also partake in that of the New, Baptism. This truth is also noted by others and generally agreed upon by modern **Theologians**, although they do not all agree on the actual meaning of this text, or regarding what truly happened to those who had already received the baptism of John. But all of Antiquity, or all the **Church Fathers** and Teachers of the Church, have been in agreement on this, and have believed with **Diodati** and several others alongside him, that those who were baptized by John also received the baptism of Christ, and that such is expressed very clearly and beyond contradiction in this 19th chapter of **Acts** <note>Acts of the Apostles, a book in the New Testament</note>. So that one has every reason to say that there was indeed such a notable, even great, distinction between these two types of Baptism, that the one could be administered to those who had already received the other; which could not have happened if they had been but one and the same baptism, and had to be regarded as such.

-> THE HOLY PART III. What this distinction may be. <-

Concerning the character or nature of their distinction, not everyone speaks with one voice; we shall recount what seems to us most in accordance with the truth and sound doctrine. **Justin Martyr** <note>c. 100–165 AD, an early Christian apologist and philosopher</note> says that the Baptism of **John** <note>John the Baptist</note> was like a forerunner to the **Gospel of grace**. In the Canons or decrees of the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 325 AD</note>, this baptism is expressly distinguished from the baptism of **Christ**. **Basil the Great** <note>330–379 AD, an influential Bishop of Caesarea and one of the Cappadocian Fathers</note>, who is praised by theologians for his insight on this, expresses himself thus in his *Exhortation to Baptism and Repentance*: "The baptism of John was for preparation, but that of Christ was for perfection; so that after this latter baptism, no other was necessary." And a little earlier he says these words: "John brought and preached the baptism of repentance; but the Lord Jesus brought and revealed the Baptism of adoption and divine sonship, which was far more excellent and glorious." Adding to this: "The former turned one away from sin, but the latter unites one with God, and allows man to enter into fellowship with Him." **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>329–390 AD, a Doctor of the Church known as "the Theologian"</note>, his friend, in his 39th Oration <note>original: "gebedt" — likely referring to his oration on the Holy Lights/Baptism</note>, and **Nicetas** <note>Nicetas of Heraclea, an 11th-century commentator on Gregory’s works</note>, his interpreter, are of the same opinion. **Hilary of Poitiers** <note>c. 310–367 AD, a Latin Father known for his defense of the Trinity</note> in his commentary on **Matthew** teaches the same and speaks in almost the same manner. **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, c. 347–407 AD, Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his eloquence</note> notes regarding the same passage that the baptism of Christ certainly included everything that was specific to that of John; but that the baptism of John did not contain all that was specific to that of **Jesus Christ**. ### PART III.

All of which, as one can see, tends toward this point: to say and to show that he <note>John the Baptist</note> was like a path and preparation for the Kingdom of grace, and for the state of the Gospel and the New Covenant <note>original: "Nieuwen Verbonts"</note> that was to be opened by Jesus Christ. From this it appears that as soon as the persons who came to him were, by the impression of his preaching, in some measure disposed to receive Jesus in their hearts, he could baptize them, and indeed truly did baptize them. ### PART III.

### Matthew at the 13th Chapter.

<margin>p. 13, 14.</margin> Dr. Essenius <note>Andreas Essenius (1618–1677), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Utrecht</note> has, following the lead of Dr. Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), the influential leader of the Dutch Further Reformation</note>, previously believed he could undeniably shut our mouths using the words that the Lord Christ spoke when He presented and explained this parable to His disciples. Before him, Dr. Gentman <note>Cornelis Gentman (1626–1696), a minister in Utrecht</note> also intended to prove his case through these same words, hoping to excuse himself and his colleagues from the faithful and earnest exercise of ecclesiastical **discipline** <term>kerckelicke Tucht: the process of correcting and potentially excommunicating church members to maintain the purity of the community</term>. It is well known that in his *Reflections on Schism*, he did not hesitate to say and establish that there are particularly three cases in which one must omit **Censure** <note>disciplinary action or excommunication</note>. 

1. When it is feared that those against whom one would wish to use it would separate themselves from the Congregation and cause a schism, as he puts it. 
2. When it is anticipated that, for the sake of those upon whom one would faithfully exercise it, persecution would be incited or troubles would be brought upon the Teachers and Congregations. 
3. When certain sins worthy of censure or the **ban** <note>excommunication</note> have become so common that they have crept through the whole body of the church. 

Indeed, he goes so far as to positively teach that in such cases, the use of the ban must be omitted because, he says, the fishing net 

<margin>p. 15.</margin> in some places is so full of such fish that are worthy of being cast away, that if one threw them all out, nothing would remain to be gathered into the vessels. And after Dr. Gentman established these three points openly and bluntly, he claimed that these same views—presented in his aforementioned *Reflections*—were supported by the entire Theological Faculty of Utrecht.

But the Lord wishes here to restrain the premature and thoughtless zeal of His servants, who, like the **Apostles**, would want to do that which does not belong to them, and to which they were neither called nor commissioned; and He teaches them thereby not to anticipate God’s time, in which the mass of the wicked shall be gathered, and entirely removed from the world, and cast into the fiery **Oven** <note>A reference to the final judgment described in Matthew 13:42.</note> which is prepared for the wicked and all the impenitent.

->*And even less to restrain the zeal and faithfulness of Christ’s Servants.*<-

Even less is it forbidden here for the **Shepherds** <note>original: "Herderen" — refers to the pastors or ministers of the church.</note> to keep watch, so that the wicked might not manage to slip into the **Church**. For even if one wished to apply this **Parable** with all force to their actions in the Church, it nevertheless remains certain that the **Weeds** were not sown in the **Field** until the **Servants** slept, just as indeed it was after the death of the **Apostles**, and when those who followed

Then, once the servant of God has recognized that the devil has devised this fraud—realizing that the devil had no power against the authority of so great a name as Christ and thus covered his deceits with that same name—a desire may arise in him to remove such men from human affairs, should he have the opportunity. But whether he ought to do so, he consults the justice of God to see if He commands or permits this, and if He wishes this to be the duty of men. This is why the servants say: *Do you want us to go and gather them?* To which Truth itself <note>A common Augustinian title for Christ.</note> responds: that man is not so situated in this life that he can be certain of what anyone will become later, even if he sees their current error. Nor can he know how that person's error might contribute to the progress of the good. Such people are not to be removed from this life, lest while trying to kill the wicked, one kills the good (which they might yet become), or harms the righteous whom the wicked might, even unwillingly, serve. One may also ask why he says: *Bind the bundles for burning:* why?</margin>them. They could easily entertain the thought of removing these people from the world and from among men, according to the opportunity and earthly power they might possess. But before they act, they seek counsel from the <term>justice of God</term> <note>The divine law or standard of right conduct.</note> to know if He gives them a command or permission for this, and if He intends for men to perform such a task. This is why they ask Him: *“Do you want us to go and gather the weeds?”* And Truth itself answers them: since man cannot know with certainty what another will become in the future, even if they are currently in error, and because those who stray—when tolerated in the world—actually serve the greater good and the refinement of the righteous, *they must not be removed from this life. For in attempting to kill the wicked, one might also kill those who could perhaps become good, or who must at least serve (even against their will) the benefit of those who are already righteous, through the wise and hidden governance of God.* One can further ask, Augustine adds, regarding the statement that the Master of the House will say to his Angels, *“Bind the weeds in bundles to burn them”*; why does it not say to bind them all into a single bundle? It is then certain that, according to the general agreement of the Church Fathers <note>original: "Kercken-leeraers"; referring to early Christian theologians and authorities</note>, one must understand the "weeds" <note>often referred to as "tares" in older Biblical translations</note> to mean the heretics or the unorthodox; and it is also certain that they cannot be excluded from this meaning. One will then not lightly say that one must let the heretics grow up in the church. Now, the heretics are certainly included among the weeds, and Jesus says that one must let the weeds grow up in the field. Thus, the field is not the Church, but the World, where heretics may—indeed, must—be tolerated.

With such and similar words, one is accustomed to answering those who want to overextend and enforce the authority of these **Church Fathers**, particularly on the subject of the **Church**; and our request is that one takes heed of this, so that one does not follow the supporters of **Babylon** <note>In Reformation rhetoric, "Babylon" was a common pejorative for the Roman Catholic Church, referencing the "Whore of Babylon" from the Book of Revelation.</note>.

Continuation of this matter through general observations on the Parable. In the same, nothing is spoken regarding the cutting off from the Church through the exercise of Church Discipline.

<margin>PART III.</margin> If he <note>Referring to the devil or the spirit of Antichrist mentioned in the broader context.</note> had wished to transform the Church of Jesus Christ into his own kingdom, he could have made people believe nothing more suited to achieve his aim than the following errors, into which some good people have partly fallen, and in which those who constitute <term>Babylon</term> <note>A biblical symbol often used by Reformation-era writers to represent a corrupt, oppressive, or false church system.</note> are entirely submerged. 

The 1st is that the consensus of the many is a sign of truth. 

The 2nd is that no one can be saved who does not gather with, or maintain church fellowship with, those who err and do evil, and thus forms one body with them. 

The 3rd is that when the vast majority in a congregation is guilty of the same sins or errors, one does not do well to punish or rebuke the guilty. 

The 4th is that Babylon, of which the Scripture speaks so much and from which it desires us to guard ourselves, does not signify those who are Christians in name only. 

The 5th is that one must separate from such people not in the body, but only in the spirit <note>This refers to the argument that one can physically remain in a corrupt church while being "spiritually" separate.</note>. 

The 6th is that those who do not form the same body of the Church with them are <term>Schismatics</term> <note>From the Dutch *Scheurmakers*, meaning those who "tear" or divide the church; a common accusation against those who left established denominations.</note>. 

**Finally, it is answered that against all this, and whatever else may be brought forward from the previous Parable <note>The Parable of the Tares (Matthew 13:24-30), where weeds are left among the wheat until the end.</note>, it is certain** that the entire Christian Church has separated itself both from Judaism and Heathenism, and from the <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God; they were condemned at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> and <term>Heretics</term>; and that it must still separate itself from the world, from those who err, and from those who—whether through the power of their customs or through the injustice of their commands and laws—lead others into sin. From this, it clearly appears that the good have not had to remain, and also have not remained, in one and the same field with the weeds until the end of the world, if <note>original: "indien"</note>

### *Explanation of the Parable of the Fishing Net.*

Regarding the Parable of the Net cast into the Sea, which brings all kinds of fish together, and which, when it is full, the fishermen pull onto the shore, where they sit down to pick out the good into their vessels and throw the bad away: It is clearly to be seen, firstly, that by this Net—as **Theophylactus** <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107) was a prominent Byzantine archbishop and influential biblical commentator whose works remained standard in the Reformation era.</note> says—the Doctrine of **Christ** and the **Apostles**, and the preaching of the **Gospel**, must be understood. III. PART serves as an answer to this: firstly, that in this passage it is not a matter of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Avontmael," the Dutch term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> or exclusion from it / but rather that it looks toward a total cutting off, not only from the company of the Faithful / but from the midst of the living / and toward a complete temporal / indeed, as some believe, an eternal destruction and rooting out / which the Apostle, in a holy zeal, wishes upon these disturbers of Christians / and people leaning toward <margin>ἀποκόψονται. <note>original Greek: "will cut themselves off." # XX. CHAPTER.

### Explanation of the Letters to the Congre-
### gations of Revelation, through which it is shown
### that what is contained in them
### in no way conflicts with the truths confirmed
### in this Book.

**A**lthough what we have just said concerning the
Revelation could give us cause to
end our answers to all that is thrown
against us from Holy Scripture, we shall
nonetheless, before we leave this subject,
examine a little more closely what some think
can be drawn against our Doctrine from the
Letters that the Lord Jesus writes in Revelation
to the seven Congregations <term>Gemeynten: The local assemblies or churches</term> of Asia; and we shall
clearly show that people wrongly imagine they
can find in these letters any excuses <note>original: "dekmantels," literally "cloaks," referring to masks or covers for one's faults</note>
for the laxity in which they live, or for the
unfaithfulness in performing one's duty to
keep oneself unspotted from the world,
so that one does not partake in its sins and
plagues. And in order to better show what the
general sense, and as it were the thread and
connection of Christ’s words in those Letters is,
we shall present them exactly as they are, and
make some observations or reflections <note>original: "reflexien"</note> upon
them that may be necessary to show the true
understanding of the same. We shall then begin
with the 20th verse of the 1st chapter of
Revelation, and thereafter proceed to the
2nd and 3rd chapters, in which these Holy Letters
are found.

<header>III. PART. The HOLY</header>

<margin>Revelation 1.</margin>
v. 20. The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands. The seven stars are the Angels of the seven congregations; and the seven lampstands which you saw are the seven congregations. <term>Gemeynten: local assemblies or church bodies</term>

### I. REFLECTION.

What is said of these congregations and their angels certainly cannot be limited to seven particular assemblies of Asia, or to their principal shepherds; as many teachers, both ancient and modern, agree with us on this. And of this we can give, among others, these reasons: <margin>Revelation 1:13.</margin> 1. Jesus, who appears here as walking in the midst of the seven lampstands, surely walks in the midst of all the congregations, which consequently are also included under this number of seven. 2. The Spirit who speaks here, speaks to them all in common, and not particularly to those seven, or privately to the others. 3. <margin>5:6.</margin> The seven Spirits (which signify that sevenfold Spirit speaking to these seven congregations) are sent out into all lands; and accordingly, the same speaks here to the entire universal church, represented by these seven particular assemblies. 4. One has only to look at the promises made to them to see that they have by no means had their full fulfillment in these congregations, which have long since been entirely destroyed or choked out <note>original: "verstropt," implying the spiritual life was stifled or the historical churches ceased to exist</note>. 5. The number seven, which is a number of fullness and perfection, and is frequently repeated here, is al-

<header>PART III. THE HOLY PLACE</header>

## 2. REFLECTION.

The Angels are distinguished here from the lampstands; therefore, although what is written to them also sometimes applies to the churches and extends to them, one must nevertheless not take them for one and the same. Instead, one must maintain the distinction that **Jesus** Himself will point out. This must especially be observed in what is said of these Angels, applying it to certain specific **Shepherds** <note>The author interprets the "Angels" of the seven churches not as celestial beings, but as the human ministers or "Shepherds" of the congregations.</note> of these particular **Assemblies** of **Asia**.

# I. Letter, written to the Angel of the Congregation of Ephesus.

### v. 1. Write to the Angel of the Congregation of Ephesus, These things says He who holds the seven stars in His right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.

<margin>
Revelation 2.
The Ephesian Church relates to the Church of the primitive times, in which—just as in that of Israel, Judges 2:7—the truth remained all the days of Joshua and the Elders who outlived Joshua; so too while the Apostles, Apostolic men, and their disciples were still living. <note>original Latin: "Ephesina Ecclesia relationem habet ad primitivorum temporum Ecclesiam, in qua, sicut in illa Israelis, Judic. 2, 7. permansit veritas omnibus diebus Joshua, ac Seniorum qui Joshua fuere superstites; ita viventibus adhuc Apostolis, virisque Apostolicis, & eorum discipulis"</note>
</margin>

## Chapter XXI.

->Response to that which is raised as an objection from the ancient or modern practice of the Church.<-

Having thus far broadly confirmed the truths we intended to prove through the Holy Scripture / and having also answered point by point everything brought against us or that could be brought against us from the same / we must now say something about the prejudice drawn from Antiquity and its authority / the vanity or powerlessness of which we demonstrated at the end of the 2nd Part of this Book. The reformation begun by Hus <note>Jan Hus (c. 1369–1415), a Bohemian reformer influenced by Wycliffe; he was burned at the stake for heresy, sparking the Hussite Wars.</note> in the year 1410 follows, which succeeded openly in the churches of Bohemia and Moravia separated from the papacy, and thereafter in the churches of Poland.

*History of the schism of the Donatists, from which it appears that those who separate themselves from idolaters, heretics, or the godless and worldly out of love for God, are wrongly compared to them.*

The first rise of the **Donatists** <note>A North African Christian movement that began in 311 AD. They believed that only "holy" people could belong to the church and that sacraments performed by "unworthy" clergy were invalid.</note> originated from the hatred and desire for revenge of a prominent woman named **Lucilla**, who, having been rebuked by **Caecilian**, <term>Deacon</term> <note>A person appointed to administrative or service roles within a church; here, a high-ranking official in Carthage.</note> of the Church of Carthage, for the habit she had of kissing the bone of a supposed Martyr before she received the <term>Lord's Supper</term> <note>original: "Avontmael." The Christian sacrament of Communion or the Eucharist.</note>, became so embittered against him that she harbored the memory of it, with the intention of avenging it if she could. 

Some time later, the opportunity for this presented itself: for **Mensurius**, <term>Bishop</term> of Carthage, having died, and this **Caecilian**—who was only a deacon—having been chosen in his place, the priests **Botrus** and **Celestius**, because they saw themselves excluded from that dignity which they had so greatly desired, formed a large faction against him. To this end, they made use of the influence and the immense wealth of **Lucilla**, who was happy that these persons gave her an opportunity to let her revenge burst forth against the one who had faithfully warned her of her duty. 

This party, having conspired together, found a means to provoke **Secundus**, <term>Primate</term> <note>The highest-ranking bishop in a specific province or region, in this case, Numidia.</note> of **Numidia**, to pride and jealousy, suggesting to him that the ordination of Caecilian was invalid because...
