# FOURTH PART.

*Wherein is shown that the doctrine and practice of the Church of Christ in the first centuries confirm the truths asserted in this book.*

---

## CHAPTER I.

### Introduction to this fourth part.

To put the finishing touches on this work, we shall—contrary to what is so commonly thought and said—show once and for all that true and pure **Antiquity** <term>Antiquity</term> <note>In this context, "Antiquity" refers to the era of the Early Church, specifically the period of the Church Fathers immediately following the Apostles.</note> is on our side. We shall therefore in this final part of this book present the words of the first teachers of the Christian church, in which one will be able to notice what the sentiments were of those who succeeded the **Apostles**, and what the constant doctrine has been of the new People that the Lord had come to form on earth for the honor of His Name.

It is true that one has very few writings from the first three centuries of the Church, either because at that time the Christians applied themselves more to doing than to speaking, and more to suffering for Christ than to writing much about Him; or because of the diligent search that the **Heathen Emperors** <note>Refers to Roman Emperors such as Diocletian, who during the "Great Persecution" (303–313 AD) specifically targeted Christian scriptures and records for destruction.</note>—above all in the final persecution—ordered for the church books, so as to snatch them out of the hands of the faithful to tear—

<summary>This page introduces the final part of the book, which seeks to prove that the author's theological positions are supported by the "pure antiquity" of the early Church. It explains the scarcity of early Christian writings as a result of the believers' focus on martyrdom and the systematic destruction of books by Roman authorities.</summary>

<header>THE HOLY. 572</header>

**PART IV.** them apart and burn them with fire, a great number of them have been lost. However, **Providence** <note>The protective care of God, viewed here as the reason why some ancient texts survived despite persecution.</note> has still preserved enough of them to allow us to see that the **Christian People**—being entirely different from what they later became, and especially from what they are now—also worked in an entirely different spirit and according to other **fundamental principles**, in order to maintain their purity and to prevent corruption and errors from gaining the upper hand among them.

One also observes that as corruptions began to grow, the faithful **Shepherds of the Church** <note>The early bishops and leaders who were seen as the spiritual guardians of their congregations.</note>—opposing them holily and with power—made several remarkable **ordinances** <term>ordinances</term> <note>In this context, these are "canons" or ecclesiastical laws established by early church councils to regulate discipline and maintain the sanctity of the community.</note> which nowadays seem very strict. They set these up as a dam against the current of the corrupt age; otherwise, through the violence of **Satan**—who sought with all his might to force his people among the **People of Jesus Christ**—everything would have been flooded in a short time.

But so that we may see more distinctly what the **Doctrine** and conduct of the Church was in those first centuries, we shall gather what remains for us to say under certain **main points**, and for each point present the most remarkable matters and words that we encounter in the writings of those ancient **Teachers** <note>Referring to the Church Fathers or "Leeraers," the influential theologians of the early Christian centuries.</note>. And from this, it will be seen that they taught many weighty truths in their time, which we have discussed and proven in this book.

## CHAPTER II.

### That the first Christians recognized none as Christians, as Brothers, or as Members of the Church of Christ, except only the true Believers and truly pious, and those who could be regarded as Saints.

The truth—that being born again, or being sanctified <note>To be "sanctified" means to be made holy or set apart for God's purposes.</note> in and through **Jesus Christ** our Lord, and being a Christian or a Member of the Church must be taken as one and the same thing—can be seen spread throughout this entire Book; and it serves as a common source from which many other truths proceed; therefore we shall confirm the same here by citing the testimonies of the Ancient Teachers, before we come to other points. Observe here, then, what we have found most emphatically regarding this matter in the writings of those who are called Church Fathers <note>Dutch: *Oudvaders*. These were the influential theologians and bishops of the first few centuries of the Christian church.</note>.

Saint **Ignatius**, a follower of the Apostles, disciple of **John**, and Shepherd <note>A common term for a Bishop or lead pastor of a local congregation.</note> of the Congregation at **Antioch**, where the Disciples first received the name of Christians, says in his letter to the Congregation of **Ephesus** these following words: *There are some who deceitfully and falsely bear the name of Christians, doing such things as are unworthy of **God**. The tree is known by its fruit, and so also shall and must the professors of Christianity*

# PART IV.

A Christian can be wretched in appearance; but not in truth.... The miserable Romans think they are raised so high only so that they might fall so much lower. We, who are esteemed and held in value for our chastity and good morals, have great right to abstain from your sinful wantonness, and to withdraw ourselves from your splendor and spectacles.... We despise the arrogance of the Philosophers, whom we hold to be corrupters, adulterers, and cruel men; and we make no account of their eloquence, which only serves to recount their own vices. We display wisdom not in our clothing, but in the soul. We do not speak of great things, but we do them, living as we live.

### The HOLY

**PART IV.** [knowl]edge of Christ, even though they know how to chatter about it with a flood of select words. For the doctrine of truth is not for the tongue, but for the life of man; and it is not accepted through the intellect and memory alone, as other sciences <term>sciences (wetenſchappen): In this period, this referred to any systematic body of knowledge or academic discipline.</term> are; rather, it is only then truly accepted when it possesses the soul entirely, reaches the depths of the heart, penetrates it, and masters all its affections. We have given the first place among our duties to the reception of the doctrine of truth, since the work of our salvation begins there; but to that end, this truth must be, as it were, poured into our hearts and become living within them, so that it is not unfruitful. But of what use is it to him then to live according to those rules? This serves to prevent his great evil from increasing, and even to cause it to diminish. What more must he then do? Besides the careful observation of these commands, he must also endure the cutting by the hand of the Physician, which indeed causes him a perceptible but <term>wholesome</term> <note>original: "heyl-ſame," meaning both healthy for the body and salvific for the soul</note> pain. Thus he speaks further on this matter in the 19th, 20th, and 21st chapters of his 252nd <term>Sermon</term> <note>This likely refers to the sermons of St. Augustine, who frequently used medical analogies for repentance</note>, in which he strives to show that one must not be satisfied with performing penance only in the heart, but that the same must also be practiced through outward deeds. This second and only penance, he says—being so defined that one can perform it but once—requires that one must give all the clearer evidence of the sincerity with which one wishes to undergo it. These exercises or acts are what is ordinarily expressed by the Greek word *<term>Exomologesis</term>* <note>original: "Exomologesis," a term used in the early Church to describe the process of public confession and formal penance</note>, which signifies the declaration by which we confess our sins to God; not as if He did not know them, but because that confession works <term>penitence</term> <note>original: "boetveerdigheyt"</note>, and penance stills the wrath of God. 

This *<term>Exomologesis</term>* then is the exercise that teaches man to humble himself, prescribing for him a way of life capable of inclining the mercy of God toward him: It even takes care to regulate him in his food and clothing, commanding him to always be in sackcloth and in ashes; to let his body become unkempt without tending to it; through a deep remorse and inward feeling over his sins, to be contrite in spirit and heart; to amend the failings of his former life, pondering them and bringing them back into his memory with sorrow; to live only on bread and plain water, in order not so much to [afflict] the body as well as the...

<margin>PART IV.</margin>But in truth, it is a matter quite capable of making an honest man <term>blush</term> <note>original: "schaemroot," literally "shame-red"</note>—to be obliged to appease an <term>offended God</term> <note>original: "beledigt God"</note>, and to put oneself in a position to regain the <term>eternal treasures</term> <note>original: "eeuwige goederen," referring to the spiritual rewards or state of grace lost through sin</note> that one has squandered through one’s own fault. Is your shame not misplaced, since you have so little of it when you sin, yet so much when you are to pray for forgiveness? For my part, I would accept no shame if it were advantageous for me to despise it, since it seems that it then says to man: "Do not look at me; it is better that you lose me than that you yourself should be lost." I well admit that it is sometimes distressing to undergo humiliation before people who will afterwards mock and laugh at you, who will take the fall of their neighbor as an occasion to exalt themselves, and who, seeing him fallen to the ground, will even have the heart to trample him with their feet. But being among your <term>Brothers</term> <note>original: "Broeders," referring to fellow members of the Christian community</note>, and among the <term>Servants of one and the same Lord</term>, who all have but one hope, one fear, one joy, and one sorrow, and who all suffer for one and the same cause, as having all but one and the same <term>Spirit</term>, which they have received from their <term>common Father</term> and common Lord; being, I say, as closely united with them as you are, why do you not look upon them as other versions of yourself? Why do you flee from those who take part in your misery, as if they were rejoicing in it? The body cannot rejoice over the evil that weighs upon one of its members. It must necessarily suffer along with its pain, and strive as much as it can toward its relief.

the HOLY

IV. PART. [which] was strictly maintained, as was practiced in the Church 
->of the second and third centuries.<-

In the fourth and fifth centuries, four stages <note>original: "trappen," meaning steps or ranks</note> of Penance were established and maintained. Those who were in the first stage were called the *Weepers* <note>original: *προσκλαίοντες*, or *prosklaiontes*</note>, and their *repentance* <note>original: *boetveerdigheyt*</note> was called *weeping* or *anticipatory weeping* <note>original: *πρόσκλαυσις*, or *prosklausis*</note>; and those who practiced this stood at the door of the house of prayer or of the Church, and with crying, tears, and by beating their breasts, they begged the people entering to pray to God for mercy on their behalf. The second stage was that of *Listening* <note>original: *ἀκρόασις*, or *akroasis*</note>, or of the *Hearers* <note>original: *ἀκροώντες*, or *akroontes*</note>, who were permitted to stand in the door of the Church and, along with the Catechumens <note>those receiving basic instruction in the faith before baptism</note>, listen to the reading and explanation of God's word; however, like the Catechumens, they were dismissed <note>sent out of the assembly</note> before the Eucharist or the Lord’s Supper was held. The third stage was *kneeling* <note>original: *ὑπόπτωσις*, or *hypoptosis*</note>, or the state of the *prostrate* <note>original: *ὑποπίπτοντες*, or *hypopiptontes*</note>, who, being knelt and bowed down in a specific place in the Church, were covered with sackcloth and ashes, and through various acts and ceremonies, demonstrated the displeasure they felt toward their sins; for this reason, their penance was also often called *Exomologesis* <note>a Greek term for public confession and discipline</note> or Confession by the ancients, as they confessed their crimes through their words and deeds, and through their extreme humiliation made it evident how deeply they grieved over them. These, after having received the blessing and the laying on of hands from the Overseer <note>original: *Opziender*, meaning the Bishop</note>, departed, without yet being allowed to be present in the Congregation during the administration of the Eucharist. The fourth and last stage was the

### for the Saints.

Standing, or the enduring **standing together** <note>original Greek: *σύστασις* (*systasis*)</note>, and those who were in this state were called **consistents** <note>original Greek: *συνισταμένοι* (*synistamenoi*), meaning those who stand together</note>; these remained in the Assembly alongside the Faithful for as long as it lasted, though they remained standing, whereas the Faithful were seated. They were also present during the prayers and the entire public service, even during the holding of the **Holy Supper** <note>the Eucharist or Communion</note>, though they did not yet partake of it. Finally, after having passed through all these stages, they were admitted to communion with all the other Faithful; this occurred through the laying on of hands by the **Bishop** or the **Priest** in the presence of the Ministers of the Word and the entire congregation. Regarding the time one had to wait to pass through all these stages, this was determined by the Rules of the **Councils**, which defined the duration according to the gravity of the sins; the shortest was three years, and sometimes it lasted up to thirty years. Furthermore, one could perform this penance for the same sin only once in a lifetime; so that if someone happened to fall again into the same fault that merited public penance, they were excluded from the communion of the Church forever. It is for this reason that **Tertullian**, in the book **On Chastity** <note>original Latin: *De Pudicitia*</note>, calls this Penance the "last hope of the Christian." It is not that they cut off all hope of God’s mercy for those who committed the same sin for which they had already satisfied through public penance; rather, it was that they did not believe such a person should be admitted a second time to the **ecclesiastical remedy** <note>the "medicine" of the formal penance process</note>, which they had held in such low regard, so as not to give sinners an occasion or freedom to continue in their sins in the hope of always [receiving] forgive-

Nevertheless, Pope **Siricius**, around the year 385, granted those who had fallen into the same sin for a second time after their first penance the right to practice and attend religious services, as well as to receive the **Eucharist** <note>the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion</note>, but only when they were on their deathbed; and it is specifically noted in that regard that the old rigor was already beginning to slacken at that time.

But let us look at the decrees concerning this matter of the **Penitents** <note>people undergoing public discipline to be readmitted to the church</note> from the famous **Council of Nicaea**, called by **Constantine the Great**, as they are recounted by **Gelasius of Cyzicus**, who wrote the history of that Council.

In the 11th **Canon** <note>a formal church law or rule</note> concerning those who had abandoned the faith purely out of worldly inclinations, the Council speaks as follows:

> *Although such people are unworthy of any compassion, the holy **Synod** <note>a gathering of church leaders to decide on doctrine or discipline</note> has nevertheless seen fit to grant them some concession or leniency. Those who show serious remorse for their sin shall be admitted among the **Hearers** <note>the first stage of penance, where the person stood in the narthex to listen to the sermon but left before the liturgy of the faithful</note> for three years; and thereafter, being placed in the order of the **Penitents**, they shall remain for seven years among the **Kneelers** <note>the second stage, where they were allowed inside the church but had to remain on their knees</note>, praying for mercy from the Faithful or members of the congregation at the entrance of the church: After which time they shall be allowed to pray with the faithful people, though without approaching the **Table of the Lord**.*

Others believe that the first period of three years was for those who had fallen during their **Catechumenate** <note>the period of instruction and trial before baptism</note>; and the seven-year penance for those who [fell] after they were among the Faithful...

For all those who, through the feeling of the fear of the Lord, through their tears, perseverance, and good works, prove the truth of their actual improvement, may, after being placed among the **Hearers** <note>the first stage of penance, where individuals stood in the back to listen to the sermon but were dismissed before the prayers of the faithful</note> for three years, be present at the prayers and share in them. After which the Overseer or Shepherd <note>a Bishop or Pastor</note> may proceed with some leniency toward them."

<margin>Others, following Rufinus in the translation of his Canons, count this as the 13th.</margin>

> "Regarding the Catechumens who happen to fall while being instructed in the holy Mysteries, it has seemed just to the holy and great Synod that they should be placed among the Hearers for only three years; and that they should pray with the Catechumens thereafter."

<margin>The Canons of the famous Council of Elvira or Eliberis in Spain.</margin>

PART IV.
[The canons] held in the Year of our Lord 306 <note>This refers to the Council of Elvira (Eliberis), known for its exceptionally rigorous discipline</note> are even stricter than those of the General Council of Nicaea, as can be seen if one takes the trouble to seek them out and compare them with one another.
</margin>

There one sees now a sample of the **Discipline** <term>tucht: the system of rules and spiritual punishments used by the early church to maintain moral purity</term> by which the Church, since the time of the Apostles of the Lord, was preserved in great purity. This discipline, while remaining in some strength for a long time, gradually slackened so sadly that Mr. J. <note>likely Pierre Jurieu, a 17th-century theologian</note> in his *Preservative*, page 202, therefore asked: "Is that terrible slackening of **Church discipline** nothing at all?" Previously, the Church imposed as punishment for scandalous deeds, a **penance** <term>boete: a period of exclusion from the sacraments and public displays of repentance</term> of ten, twenty, even thirty years. The fear of being separated for such a long time from the use of holy things was a bridle that curbed the violence of the passions. These long-lasting penances were performed in public; and the fear of having one's crimes exposed to everyone was yet another means to stem the madness of lustful desires. But today, one sees almost no trace of it anymore.

To give an even more perfect understanding of **Penitence** <term>Boete: both the act of repenting and the formal ritual of reconciliation</term> and of the feelings with which the Penitent ought to be imbued while they are undergoing the same, we shall bring forward several memorable words from Tertullian, Cyprian, and Chrysostom <note>Three influential "Church Fathers" from the 2nd to 4th centuries</note>, who specifically dealt with this subject. See here how the first, namely **Tertullian**, speaks of the **penitence** which he calls "the second" <note>Tertullian distinguished between the first repentance (at baptism) and a single "second chance" for repentance for sins committed after baptism</note>, in distinction from the first, which was for the **Catechumens** <note>those receiving instruction in the faith before being baptized</note> who did penance for their previous life led according to the spirit of this world. <margin>PART IV.</margin> GOD is no respecter of persons. In the church there is neither servant nor free man: She recognizes no servants except those who are servants of sin, according to the word of Christ, *He who commits sin is a servant of sin;* and she also recognizes no free men except those who have been made free by grace, according to these words, *The law of the spirit of life which is in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin.*

Do you believe He will be able to forgive you easily, after you have denied or rejected Him as your God and Lord?

One must pray to God constantly and with zeal. One must spend one's days in tears. One must keep watch and weep through the night. One must devote all one's time to sighing and weeping. One must lie down upon the earth. One must cover oneself with a hair shirt <term>hayren kleet; a garment made of coarse, itchy animal hair worn to cause physical discomfort as an act of humility</term> and with ashes. After losing Jesus Christ, with whom one was once clothed, one should no longer desire any worldly garment. After having eaten of the devil’s food <note>original: "spijse des duyvels"; referring to meat sacrificed to Roman idols, which Christians were forced to eat to prove they had renounced Christ</note>, one must love nothing more than fasting. One must keep busy with good works, through which one is freed from one's sins. One must often give alms <term>aelmoessen; charitable gifts to the poor</term>, through which souls are delivered from death. Jesus Christ must receive what the enemy sought to take from you. And after being deceived and conquered by riches, one must no longer love or keep them.

One must regard earthly possessions as an enemy; one must flee them like a robber; and one must fear and sell them like the sword that has wounded us: make great and constant gifts of charity from them.

You object, he says, that **Novatus** <note>original: "Novatus"; likely referring to Novatian, the 3rd-century leader of a rigorist schism who refused to readmit Christians who had sacrificed to idols under threat of death.</note> did not receive those who had fallen under the persecution. And even if I do accept them, I give them a place according to the requirement of the state in which they are; but if I find them completely transformed by their tears, then I shall not follow him in rejecting them.

**Ambrose**, that renowned <term>Overseer; Opsiender, a Dutch term for a Bishop</term> of **Milan**, expresses himself thus in the 16th chapter of the 1st book that he wrote against the **Novatians**, regarding the treatment that must be maintained over penitent souls, not admitting them too easily or too loosely to **Communion**. If anyone, he says, having committed deadly, covered, and hidden sins, afterwards performs penance for them with diligence and zeal, in order to fulfill the command of the Lord **Jesus**; how does he receive the reward thereof, if he is not restored again into the communion of the **Church**, and admitted to the enjoyment of the holy **Lord's Supper**? There are some, he says in the 9th chapter of the 2nd book <note>Referring to Book II of Ambrose's "De Poenitentia" (On Penance).</note>, who desire penance only so that they may be admitted immediately back to the **Communion** from which they are excluded. Such persons wish more to bind their <term>Pastors; Herders, the spiritual leaders of the congregation</term> than to be unbound themselves. ...innocence they had when they were baptized, or as I have met those who, after having lost it, have performed a proper <term>penance; Boetveerdigheyt, a state of deep remorse and discipline</term>. Does one think that True Penance exists where there is ambition, where one chases after high offices, where there is luxury, and where one makes good cheer, or where the use of marriage remains as it was before? One must renounce the world. One must give less time to sleep than nature requires. One must interrupt one's rest with supplications, and mingle it with sighs. One must spend part of that time in prayers. One must live in such a way that one dies to the vain habits of this life. Let a man deny himself and change himself completely.

Let us take great care, *he says elsewhere (writing on the 119th Psalm)*, that we do not make those to whom we show mercy without cause even worse. There is often more severity in not punishing sinners than there is in punishing them. ... Even in the Church, in which one must work with great long-suffering and kindness, one must maintain the form and the rule of justice very precisely regarding the Penitent. This is so that the one who is separated from the enjoyment of the <term>Holy Supper; het heylige Avontmael, also known as the Eucharist or Communion</term> is not too quickly or too easily granted the freedom to receive it again by the <term>Shepherds; the local pastors or bishops</term> through short-lived or passing tears, or even through a great flood of weeping. This freedom should not be granted to him until after he has prayed for it for a long time. For when the Shepherd slackens, granting the same to an unworthy person, does he not then encourage others to...

...unworthy to follow him in his sins and in his fall? Too great an ease in forgiving makes people prone to sinning. I say this, so that we should know that the mercy of God must be administered only according to the word of God and according to justice. If a <term>Physician; Genees-meester</term> sees that <term>cancer; kancker, here likely meaning a spreading infection or gangrene</term> is entering a wound, and if he then, allowing himself to be moved by the tears of the patient, neglects to cut (so that the evil does not increase) and does not burn out the rotten flesh, but only applies some plasters to that which he should have opened with the knife; is that mercy and gentle handling not then evil and harmful, since to avoid the short pain of cutting or cauterizing, the whole body is corrupted and life is lost? It is then with good reason that a <term>Shepherd; Herder, referring to a pastor or bishop</term>, like a good <term>Surgeon; Heel-meester</term>, should cut a great wound out of the body of the Church, and drive out the hidden <term>poison; fenijn</term> of sin instead of nurturing it, so that by not excluding one person from the communion of the church, he does not make many others worthy of being excluded from it.

In his 24th Sermon on 1 Cor. 10, he also says these remarkable words: *Wherever the dead body shall be, there shall the eagles be gathered.* <note>original: "Alwaer het doode lichaem sal zijn, daer sullen sich de arenden vergaderen." This is a reference to Matthew 24:28, which Chrysostom interprets allegorically regarding the Eucharist.</note> The Body of the Son of God is called the "dead body" because of the death He suffered. For if Christ had not risen, then we too would not rise. And those who approach this Body are called **Eagles**, to show that they must be noble and elevated souls, who have nothing to do with the earth, who do not lean downward, and who do not crawl in the unclean love of the creatures; but who continually fly up toward the things that are above, and whose spirit, with a sharp vision and piercing eyes, gazes firmly and unmovably upon the **Sun of Righteousness**. For that Table is the table of the **Eagles** and not of the ravens. Elsewhere, namely in his Homily on the prodigal Son, he explains those words / *I am not worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants*, thus: *Drive me not away from your house, Lord, so that the enemy might not find me wandering and roaming about, and drag me away with him and make me his slave. But do not let me approach your hidden and awesome Table; for I would not have the boldness to look upon the Holy of Holies with unclean eyes. # CHAPTER XV.

THE Doctrine <note>Referring to the reformed or Waldensian teachings.</note> that God had preserved and renewed among those good people from the Valleys of Piedmont <note>The Waldensians lived in the Alpine valleys of the Piedmont region.</note>, having been spread in France and especially in the Provinces of Languedoc, Guienne, and Picardy, was even—as some Historians point out—known as far as England and there accepted by John Wycliffe; likewise in Italy and Germany, where it found many followers. But it was especially propagated in Bohemia by Jan Hus <note>A Czech priest and philosopher who became a church reformer and the predecessor to Protestantism.</note> and Jerome of Prague, and by their upright disciples the Taborites <note>The Taborites were a radical faction of the Hussite movement in 15th-century Bohemia.</note>; and later by the Brethren of the Bohemian Unity <note>original: "Boheemsche Eenigheyt"; also known as the Unitas Fratrum, the predecessors of the Moravian Church.</note>, who, being spread in this Kingdom as well as in Poland and Moravia, have extended their dying remnants until these our days. We shall bring forward various matters concerning this Brotherhood in this chapter, which are suitable to confirm the truths contained in this Book.

### CHAPTER XV.

->*In which it is shown that the Churches of the United*<-
->*Brethren of Bohemia bear witness to our*<-
->*doctrine and practice.*<-

The Doctrine which God had preserved and renewed among those good people from the Valleys of Piedmont—having been spread throughout France and particularly in the provinces of Languedoc, Guyenne, and Picardy—became known even as far as England, as some historians indicate, and was there embraced by *John Wycliffe* <note>original: "Joannes Wiclef," an influential 14th-century English theologian whose followers were known as Lollards.</note>; likewise in *Italy* and *Germany*, where the same found many followers. But it was especially propagated in *Bohemia* by *Jan Hus* <note>original: "Joannes Hus," the Czech reformer whose execution in 1415 sparked the Hussite Wars.</note> and *Jerome of Prague*, and by their sincere disciples, the *Taborites* <note>A radical faction of the Hussite movement that sought to live according to their interpretation of the simplicity of the early Church.</note>; and later by the Brethren of the *Bohemian Unity* <term>Unitas Fratrum: a Christian denomination that emerged from the Hussite movement, emphasizing communal living and strict adherence to the Bible.</term>, who, being spread throughout this Kingdom as well as in *Poland* and *Moravia*, have extended their dying remnants even unto our present days. We shall bring forward various matters concerning this Brotherhood in this chapter, which are suitable to confirm the truths contained in this book.

were / of which the first were called the "beginners" / the second the "advanced" / the third those "stretching out toward perfection" / and the fourth kind were the **Penitents** <term>Penitents: "Boetveerdige," members undergoing formal church discipline for sins, temporarily separated from full communion.</term> / who, having fallen into some particular faults / through the church / according to its old practice which we have seen here before / were placed in a state of penance.

<margin>Art. 16. 17, 18 * <note>original: "Unde fit ut quemadmodum mali à bonis hac in Ecclesia removeantur, ita lapsi à firmioribus sejūgūtur, ad evidentiorem Ecclesiae ædificationem quorum nihil alibi videas, ubi nullo res geruntur ordine, pares sunt omnes inter se nec ater differt ab albo."</note> From this it follows that just as the wicked are removed from the good in this Church, so the fallen are separated from the steadfast, for the clearer edification of the Church; of which you see nothing elsewhere, where things are conducted without order, where everyone is equal to one another and black does not differ from white.</margin>

PART IV. ...which Jesus Christ is the first-born [in]; why He shall say to his Father,

It is in this respect that the Apostle says in Galatians 3:26 <note>Original citation: "Gal. 3: 2, 6"; likely a printer's error for 3:26</note>: *For you are all Children of God through faith in Christ Jesus.* And Galatians 4:6: *Moreover, because you are children, God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.*

He who loves his own wife, loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, but he nourishes it and cherishes it, even as the Lord does the Church. I shall add two things to all these considerations: **CHAPTER XVI.**
The first is, that the Church is called <term>Militant</term> <note>original: "Strijden-de"; referring to the "Church Militant," the body of believers currently living and "fighting" against sin on earth.</note>, as long as she is here below, because she fights against the devil, the world, sin, and the flesh, and every day nobly exerts force against the vices that oppose the work of her sanctification, which she desires to complete in the fear of God, in order to afterwards be crowned with glory and immortality. From which it necessarily follows, that all those who are slaves to their sensual or carnal lusts, and who allow themselves to be mastered by their passions and desires, are not of this Militant Church; and just as they are not of that Church which struggles upon the earth, they shall also not be of that which <term>triumphs</term> <note>original: "triumpheert"; referring to the "Church Triumphant," the believers who have died and are now in heaven with God.</note> in Heaven. In this spiritual war, we have Hope as a Helmet, Righteousness as a Breastplate, Faith as a Shield, Peace as Footwear, the word of God as a Sword, and that which makes these weapons complete is Prayer, the practice of which is at all times useful and healthy for us. These weapons are not for the use of the evil and hypocritical; the true Believers alone are clothed with them; the Believers, I say, <margin>*1 Peter 2:11*</margin> *who as sojourners and strangers, abstain from fleshly lusts, which wage war against the soul.*

The second thing I observe is, that in the *Apostles' Creed* <note>original: "Symbolum der Apostelen"</note>, which is common to all Christians, the article of the Church is explained by that of the *Communion of Saints*, where it is said, *I believe in one holy Universal Church, the <term>Communion of Saints</term>.* <note>original: "Gemeynschap der Heyligen"</note>. -># THE HOLY<-

**PART IV.** ...that all the obligations into which we enter, and which **God** imposes on us, do not only regard ourselves—insofar as we act or perform any deed in or for ourselves, or without regard for others—but that there is a great number of obligations which are grounded solely on the commitments we have toward others. Regarding these, it is certain that we act either well or poorly according to **God** and His divine will, or according to our own conceptions, discretion, and self-interest. And according to this, it is also true that we either sin and defile ourselves before the Face of the **Lord**, or we do our duty and keep ourselves undefiled in His holy presence.

Whoever would want to deny this premise would overthrow all natural, civil, and ecclesiastical or supernatural <term>fellowship<note>original: "gemeynschap," referring to the shared bonds and mutual responsibilities within a community</note></term>, destroy its foundations, and break all its bonds. And by doing so, one would also go directly against everything that the **Scripture** says so often on this point, and make oneself worthy of being suppressed by all the powerful words it has spoken in this regard.

This then being established beforehand, it appears clearly that through the enjoyment of the **Lord's Supper** and the holding of that holy meal, one can sin in two ways: namely, either in that which regards us in particular, or in our duty and commitment toward those with whom we eat and <term>communicate<note>original: "communiceeren," the act of sharing in the sacrament together</note></term>. For if we do it with those with whom we should not do it, who will then be able to acquit us of unfaithfulness and transgression, and

<margin>Chapter XVI.</margin>
...can we relieve our souls of sin, and our hearts and consciences of <term>defilement<note>original: "besmettinge," referring to a spiritual or ritual contamination caused by association with sin</note></term>? For the one necessarily flows from the other. Sin is the staining of our soul; and if one follows it through unfaithfulness, it usually drags so many contagious and guilt-inducing consequences with it that it cannot be sufficiently stated or expressed. Therefore, wherever one recognizes that sin is present, one must also necessarily admit that defilement is present there. And therefore, if it is true—as it certainly is—that one can sin by giving the **Lord's Supper** to others, or receiving it from their hands, or simply holding it with them, then it is very absurd to ask how one can be defiled by <term>communicating<note>original: "communiceeren," here meaning the act of sharing the sacrament of the Eucharist together</note></term> with others. 

Now, it is certain that one sins if one does so with those with whom one should not, and with whom it is not permitted to eat this holy meal by virtue of the laws of **God** and **Jesus Christ**. This cannot be disputed or denied. And consequently, how many persons will find themselves guilty in this matter, according to the laws of **God** which we have presented regarding this in this book, and which are clearly and sufficiently known? And how many are there not who should be ashamed and humbled, seeing that they have given this sign of the **Christian fellowship** to, and taken it with, those from whom they should have stayed far away in taking it, and to whom they should have been very careful not to give it?

Now, one sees in those same words how much one is obliged to withdraw from those who do not have the truth of **Christ** in them, and how very holily cautious one must be not to give them any testimonies of <term>fellowship<note>original: "gemeynschap," referring to spiritual communion or shared religious identity</note></term>. One partakes in their evil state if one testifies to being united with them; and if that evil is sufficiently known to us as such, then it is clear that one must take great care to avoid doing things regarding them that constitute a hidden approval of what we ought to condemn, and against which we are obliged to bear faithful witness.

When the Apostle **Paul** commands his disciple **Timothy** on behalf of the Lord to lay hands on no one hastily, <note>Referring to the rite of ordination or the appointment of church leaders (1 Timothy 5:22).</note> he adds these remarkable words: **And have no fellowship in the sins of others: Keep yourself pure.** From which one can see without difficulty that, in order not to defile oneself before God, one must not only pay attention to what we do for ourselves, but also to what we do regarding others; and that if one, through <term>faint-heartedness<note>original: "slaphertigheyt," implying a lack of moral courage or spiritual resolve</note></term>, negligence, or unfaithfulness, gives him the testimonies of approval that one should have...

# INDEX

Contains three great mysteries in which the whole of Christianity is enclosed. 3-6.
Wrong sentiments of various denominations regarding the same. 7, 8.
What it signifies and seals to true Communicants. <note>original: "Communicanten"; refers to those authorized to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper.</note> 9-11.
Who may approach the same, and who may not. 19, 20. 23-27.
Its similarity to, and distinction from, the Passover. <note>original: "Pascha." The author draws parallels between the Jewish Passover and the Christian Lord's Supper.</note> 34-37. 39, 40.
Does not impart grace, but signifies and seals the same. 42. <note>This reflects a Reformed theological view that the bread and wine are signs and seals of grace already received, rather than the physical means of obtaining it.</note>
That unholy and unconverted persons must be kept away from the same, is proven.
Firstly, from several grounds of the Old Testament, such as:
1. That the Priests might not allow any uncircumcised, strangers, or unclean persons to the Passover. 34-39.
2. That before eating the Passover, all leaven had to be swept out. 43-45.
3. That the Priests might not allow any lepers or unclean persons to the holy things. 46-51.
Secondly, from the words of Jesus Christ, forbidding:
1. Giving the Holy thing to the dogs. 52-58. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6.</note>
2. Casting the bread of the Children before them. 59-61.
Thirdly, from the words of the Apostles.
1. From 1 Cor. 5. 62-67.
2. From 1 Cor. 10: 16, 17. 67-70.
3. From 2 Thess. 3. 71-73.
The Lord's Supper is a testimony of mutual Fellowship. <note>original: "Gemeynschap." Can also be translated as "Communion" or "Community."</note> 67, 68, 84.
The erring and ignorant must not be admitted there. 74-81.
Nor those who appear to be without fear and love of the Lord. 82-85.
One must not hasten to admit those who give no sufficient evidence of worthiness. 85-90.
To give the same to the unworthy is like justifying the wicked and declaring the guilty to be innocent. 100, 101.
Those who give no evidence of grace may rightfully be kept from it. 102.
If the same cannot be held except with wicked and offensive people, then it may, indeed must, be omitted. 121-123.
It may no more be held with the wicked than with heretics and idol-worshippers, whether this happens in a true or in a false Church. 116, 117. 121. 126.
Even true Believers must be kept from the same when they commit considerable sins, until their repentance be made manifest. 207.
It is better to suspend the same for a time than to distribute it poorly. 253-255.
What kind of persons the Apostles admitted to the same. 480, 481.
How it was held in the primitive Church. 492, 493.
It is a food for the strong. 27, 655, 656, 667, 668.
By admitting the unworthy, according to the teaching of the Heidelberg Catechism, the Covenant of God is profaned, and His wrath is kindled against the entire Congregation. 96, 728. <note>The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) is a foundational document for the Dutch Reformed Church; Question 82 specifically addresses this issue of barring the ungodly from the Lord's Supper.</note>

### TERTULLIAN <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage, often cited regarding church discipline.</note>

Teaches that the true Saints are only Christians. 582, 583.
Treats the first Repentance. <term>Boetveerdigheyt</term> 601-603. <note>Penitence or repentance; in the early church, this often referred to a formal, public process of reconciliation after a serious sin.</note>
His remarkable words on the second Repentance. 624, 6<unclear>26</unclear>
Speaks of the duty of the Ministers in exercising Discipline against the unworthy. 671, 672.
Shows that the heretics were also distinguished from the true Church in this, that they had no right Church Discipline. 704.

### THEOPHILUS <note>Likely Theophilus of Antioch, a 2nd-century Christian writer.</note>

Declares that no one is a Christian but he who is anointed with the Holy Spirit. 579.

### DISCIPLINE <note>original: "Tucht." Specifically "Church Discipline," the system of monitoring and correcting the behavior of church members.</note>

The basis and the possibility of its practice. 157-215.
When it must not be practiced in the Churches, according to the opinion of Dr. Gentman. <note>Cornelis Gentman (1626–1704), a Dutch Reformed theologian known for his views on church order.</note> 402.
The same would have to be entirely abolished when the Parable of <insert>the weeds is applied...</insert>

## THE PRINCIPAL MATTERS.

[that] the weeds <note>original: "onkruyt." This concludes the entry from the previous page regarding the Parable of the Tares/Weeds.</note> must be applied to the exercise of the same <note>the "exercise of the same" refers to church discipline.</note> regarding unworthy communicants. 445-450.
The opinion of Bucerus <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a Protestant Reformer who heavily influenced views on church discipline.</note> regarding its necessity. 482-490.
Upon the faithful exercise of the same depends the good condition of a Congregation. 549.
[Discipline] was exercised even upon the Emperors in the first centuries. Various beautiful opinions concerning this. 674-686. <note>Likely referring to Saint Ambrose's refusal to admit Emperor Theodosius to the Eucharist until he repented of a massacre.</note>
The Discipline <term>Tucht</term> of the first centuries of Christianity. See the entire fourth Part.
Discipline of the Waldensians. 690-695. <note>A pre-Reformation Christian movement known for strict moral living.</note>
Discipline of the Churches of Bohemia. 700. etc. <note>Referring to the Bohemian Brethren.</note>

### TEMPORARY BELIEVERS.

That one can give the Lord’s Supper <term>Avontmael</term> to them with a good conscience does not excuse anyone who gives it to public sinners. 69, 70.
They are recognizable when they believe as well as when they fall away. 144-146.
A Congregation does not sin if it gives the Lord's Supper to such people before their falling away. 146.
Distinction between these and true Believers. 147, 148.
What one may call them, as long as they are such. 148.
Which matters they have in common in some way with the true Believers. 149.

->V.<-

### COVENANT.

After the destruction of the Old [Covenant], nothing similar has been instituted again, and who seeks to do so. 280-282.
That which gave right and entrance into the Old [Covenant] does not give such in the New. 282.
That no one but only the true Believers have part in the New, or are Members of the Church of the New Testament, is proven:
1. From its own nature, and from all the words of Christ, the Prophets, and Apostles who speak of it. 286-292.
2. From all the texts of the Old Testament that describe to us the People of the Messiah and of the New Covenant <term>Verbont</term>. 292-303.
3. From the words of the Evangelists, and from the Teaching of Jesus Christ. 304-314.
4. From all the scriptural passages of the New Testament that describe that People. 314-327.
5. From the formation and establishment of the primitive Churches. 317-339.

### MYSTERY.

There are great mysteries <term>verborgentheyden</term> enclosed in the Holy Lord's Supper. 3-6.

### ASSEMBLIES.

In those of the primitive Church, one did not admit all kinds of persons without distinction to the hearing of the Word, the prayers, and the administration of Baptism. 635-639.

### VOETIUS.

His opinion on the separation. 552-555. <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a leading Dutch Reformed theologian known for his defense of church orthodoxy and discipline.</note>

# INDEX

## W.

### WALDENSIANS. <note>A pre-Reformation Christian movement known for their desire to return to Apostolic simplicity and their frequent persecution by the medieval Church.</note>

Their opinion on the unjust administration of the Sacraments. 681.
Regarding the Lord’s Supper <term>Avontmael</term>, and the true communicants. 681, 682.
Of the Antichrist, his works with which he covers himself, and how the Believers must separate themselves from them. 682-688.
What the cause of their separation was. 688, 689.
What they felt regarding the love of the world. 689.
How their life and conduct was. 690, 691.
Their opinion of Church Discipline <term>Kerckelicke Discipline</term>, and how they practiced it. 691-695.

### WALENBURCH BROTHERS. <note>Adrian and Peter von Walenburch, 17th-century Catholic auxiliary bishops and controversialists who wrote extensively against the Protestant Reformation.</note>

Accuse the first Reformers by the Parable of the Tares <note>original: "onkruyt." A reference to Matthew 13, often used in debates about whether "weeds" (sinners) should be allowed to remain in the church.</note>. 453-455.

### WALAUES. <note>Antonius Walaeus (1573–1639), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Leiden University who played a role at the Synod of Dort.</note>

His opinion on keeping the unworthy from the Lord’s Supper. 254.

### REBIRTH. <term>Wedergeboorte</term> <note>In a theological sense, this refers to spiritual regeneration or being "born again."</note>

Various signs of the same. 353-375.

### THE REBORN.

Are in truth and before God alone the Members of the Church, and must consequently also alone be held as such. 236-238.
That some defects and miseries still remain in them in this life. 375, 376.

### THE WORLD.

Cannot properly know and distinguish persons according to their state, nor even the hypocrites. 157-159.
Can nonetheless have some general knowledge of good and evil. 159, 160.
In what sense this word is used in the Holy Scriptures. 420.
One must separate oneself from the same, and not communicate with it. 677, 678.

### WORLDLY PEOPLE.

Can be known as such. 139-143.

### WITZIUS. <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a famous Dutch theologian known for his work on the "Covenants" and for attempting to bridge the gap between various theological factions.</note>

His opinion on the mere outward observation of the Law. 280.

### YVES or YVON. <note>Likely referring to Pierre Yvon (1646–1707), who succeeded Jean de Labadie as the leader of the Labadists, a radical separatist Pietist group.</note>

Regarding the practice of Discipline. 673, 674.
